title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO USE YOU… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING THE VERY PEOPLE HE SENT YOU TO LOVE?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO USE YOU… BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN IGNORING THE VERY PEOPLE HE SENT YOU TO LOVE?

You’re waiting for a divine assignment, a bigger platform, a powerful calling. But what if your greatest opportunity to serve Jesus has been sitting across the dinner table, sending unanswered messages, or silently falling apart right beside you?
There is a prayer that sounds beautiful in church but can become painfully uncomfortable when God begins answering it.
“Lord, use me.”
Three simple words.

You whisper them during worship. You repeat them when a sermon stirs your heart. You pray them when you see missionaries reaching the lost, pastors preaching to thousands, and testimonies of lives dramatically transformed.
“Lord, I’m available. Send me. Use my life for Your glory.”
And you mean it.
At least, you believe you do.
But then your mother calls while you're busy.
You see her name on the screen.
You silence the phone.
Your father tries to start a conversation, but you're already thinking about something else.
Your spouse needs someone to listen, but you give another distracted answer.
Your child asks you to spend a little time together, and you promise, “Later.”
A friend sends a message that says, “Are you free? I really need someone to talk to.”
You read it.
You intend to respond.
Three days pass.
Meanwhile, you're still praying for God to open doors.
Still asking Him to reveal your purpose.
Still wondering when your ministry will begin.
And somewhere between your prayers for a greater calling and your neglect of ordinary people, a question begins to rise.
What if God has already opened a door, but it doesn't look important enough for you to walk through?
What if the person you've been overlooking is someone God is calling you to love?
What if you've been searching for a mission field while stepping over the needs of the people closest to you?
And what if the most spiritually significant thing you could do today isn't something thousands of people will see?
What if it's something only one hurting person will remember?
That question should make us uncomfortable.
Not because serving publicly is wrong.
Not because dreaming of doing great things for God is sinful.
But because we can become so fascinated with the idea of being used by God that we forget what being used by God actually requires.
Love.
Not merely the language of love.
Not the appearance of compassion.
Not the reputation of being a devoted Christian.
Actual love.
The kind that interrupts your schedule.
The kind that costs you convenience.
The kind that listens when nobody is applauding.
The kind that notices suffering even when there is nothing to gain from noticing.
And Scripture gives us a devastating picture of what happens when religious activity becomes disconnected from mercy.
Jesus tells a story in Luke 10:25–37.
A man is traveling from Jerusalem to Jericho when robbers attack him. They strip him, beat him, and leave him half dead.
He is lying beside the road.
Wounded.
Helpless.
Unable to rescue himself.
Then a priest comes along.
A religious man.
Someone associated with worship, sacrifice, and the things of God.
He sees the wounded traveler.
And passes by on the other side.
Then a Levite arrives.
Another man connected with Israel's religious life.
He sees the suffering man too.
And he also passes by.
Read that carefully.
They saw him.
The problem wasn't that the suffering was invisible.
The problem was that seeing him did not lead them to stop.
Scripture does not tell us what they were thinking. We cannot honestly claim they were rushing to a worship service or protecting their schedules.
Jesus doesn't give us their excuses.
He gives us their actions.
They saw.
They passed by.
And then a Samaritan came.
Someone Jesus' original Jewish audience would not automatically have expected to become the moral example in the story.
The Samaritan saw the wounded man.
And something happened inside him.
Luke 10:33 says, in the Greek text:
καὶ ἰδὼν ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
Kai idōn esplanchnisthē.
“And when he saw him, he had compassion.”
That Greek verb, esplanchnisthē, comes from a word associated with the inward parts of the body. In this context, it describes deep, heartfelt compassion.
Not casual sympathy.
Not a polite expression of concern.
Compassion that moved him to act.
The Samaritan approached the wounded man, treated his wounds, placed him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and arranged for his continued care.
His compassion became costly.
He gave time.
He gave attention.
He gave resources.
He accepted inconvenience.
And Jesus ended the story with a command that still confronts us today:
“Go, and do thou likewise.” — Luke 10:37, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not tell the lawyer who had questioned Him to wait until he became influential enough to love people.
He did not say that mercy only matters when performed before a crowd.
He did not say that compassion requires a microphone, a ministry title, or a social media following.
He told him to go and do likewise.
And suddenly, the story isn't only about a wounded traveler on an ancient road.
It's about the person you keep walking past.
The family member whose loneliness you've stopped noticing.
The friend whose jokes have become a hiding place for pain.
The elderly neighbor who rarely receives visitors.
The coworker whose behavior irritates you, without you knowing what they are carrying.
The person who has been quietly hoping someone would ask, “Are you really okay?”
And perhaps, most painfully, the people who live under the same roof as you.
Because sometimes the easiest people to neglect are the ones whose presence we've begun taking for granted.
We assume they'll understand.
We assume they'll wait.
We assume there will always be another conversation, another dinner, another birthday, another opportunity to say what should have been said years ago.
But time is not a possession we control.
And love repeatedly postponed can become love never expressed.
There may be someone in your life who doesn't need another impressive explanation of Christianity.
They need to experience the patience Christianity teaches.
They don't need you to win another argument.
They need you to apologize.
They don't need you to quote another verse about forgiveness while refusing to acknowledge the harm you've caused.
They need you to humble yourself.
They don't need a perfect Christian standing in front of them.
They need a sincere Christian willing to sit beside them.
And that brings us to a truth we would rather avoid.
Sometimes the greatest obstacle to our witness isn't that people haven't heard what we believe. It's that they haven't seen enough of it in how we treat them.
Jesus said in John 13:35:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — KJV
The identifying mark He emphasized was love among His disciples.
Not popularity.
Not eloquence.
Not the size of an audience.
Love.
In the Greek, the word is ἀγάπη (agapē), a word that, in this context, points to the love Jesus commands His followers to demonstrate toward one another.
This love isn't measured merely by the intensity of our feelings.
It is revealed through our conduct.
Through patience.
Through service.
Through forgiveness.
Through the willingness to seek another person's good even when doing so requires sacrifice.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
You can post a beautiful Bible verse and still speak cruelly to your family.
You can share a powerful sermon and still ignore someone who needs your presence.
You can defend Christian truth online and still refuse to make peace with someone you've wounded.
You can pray passionately for revival while resisting the repentance God is calling you to practice in your own home.
None of those contradictions makes the Bible less true.
But they should make us examine whether we're allowing that truth to transform us.
Because Christianity was never meant to become a performance we maintain while our relationships quietly collapse.
James 1:22 warns:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” — KJV

And in James 2:15–17, the apostle gives an example of someone lacking clothing and daily food. Speaking words of blessing without supplying what is needed exposes the emptiness of a faith that produces no practical response.
James is not teaching that we purchase salvation through charitable acts.
He is confronting the contradiction of professing faith while remaining indifferent to the needs before us.
Genuine faith bears fruit.
And sometimes that fruit looks remarkably ordinary.
A meal prepared for someone exhausted.
A sincere apology.
A hospital visit.
A debt forgiven.
A message answered.
A grieving friend accompanied through a difficult night.
A parent treated with dignity.
A child given undivided attention.
A person struggling with sin approached with truth and gentleness rather than contempt.
Small acts, perhaps.
But not small to the people receiving them.
Imagine a woman sitting alone at her kitchen table.
She has spent the entire day trying to appear strong.
Nobody knows she cried in the bathroom at work.
Nobody knows she's terrified about the bills.
Nobody knows that the silence in her house has become almost unbearable.
Her phone lights up.
A message appears.
“Hey, you've been on my mind. How are you really doing?”
She stares at the screen.
For a moment, she doesn't know what to write.
Then she types:
And a conversation begins.
You may never know what that conversation prevented.
You may never see the full impact of the compassion you offered.
You may never receive a public thank-you.
But love does not become worthless simply because it remains unseen.
And no, this does not mean every unexpected thought about someone is a supernatural message from God.
We should be careful not to claim divine revelation where Scripture gives us no such certainty.
But we don't need a special revelation to obey a command God has already given.
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2, KJV
There is already enough in that command to keep us busy for a lifetime.
Yet there is another danger here.
Some people will read a message about loving others and immediately feel crushed.
Because they are already exhausted.
Already giving.
Already carrying responsibilities that seem heavier than their strength.
Perhaps you're the one who answers every call.
The one who helps everyone.
The one who feels guilty whenever you rest.
And you've been taught that saying no means you're failing God.
Please hear this carefully.
Biblical love is not the same as having no boundaries.
Jesus Himself withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16).
He rested.
He did not satisfy every demand people placed upon Him.
You are not the Savior of everyone around you.
Jesus is.
You cannot meet every need, solve every crisis, or be available every moment.
Loving someone does not require enabling abuse, tolerating ongoing harm, or abandoning your responsibilities.
Sometimes faithful love means helping.
Sometimes it means telling the truth.
Sometimes it means setting a necessary boundary.
Sometimes it means directing someone toward appropriate professional care or other support you cannot personally provide.
The call is not to become indispensable.
The call is to become faithful.
And faithfulness begins with surrender.
Not the surrender of pretending you're limitless.
The surrender of admitting that your time, your attention, your gifts, and your relationships belong under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you've been asking God for a larger assignment.
There is nothing wrong with that prayer.
The apostle Paul carried a calling that took him across cities and regions. The Gospel is meant to go to the nations.
But a desire for a wider reach must never become an excuse for withholding love from the people already within our reach.
Consider the story of Andrew in John 1:40–42.
Andrew encountered Jesus.
And one of the first things he did was find his brother Simon.
He brought Simon to Jesus.
We know Simon by the name Jesus gave him: Peter.
Think about that.
Andrew did not begin by addressing a stadium.
He began by bringing his brother.
We cannot reduce Peter's entire calling to Andrew's action, because Jesus Himself called and formed Peter.
But Andrew's simple act of bringing someone close to him into the presence of Christ mattered.
And it raises a question worth carrying into your own life.
Who is your Simon?
Who is the person you can encourage toward Jesus, not by pressuring or manipulating them, but by loving them faithfully and speaking the truth when the opportunity comes?
Perhaps it is your brother.
Perhaps your sister.
Perhaps a friend who has quietly walked away from church.
Perhaps a spouse who has heard your Christian vocabulary for years but longs to see greater tenderness in your character.
Perhaps someone who doesn't believe in God at all.
You cannot force another person to believe.
You cannot manufacture repentance.
You cannot convert a human soul through clever words.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
But you can bear witness to Christ.
You can pray.
You can listen.
You can serve.
You can speak with gentleness and respect.
You can invite someone to read Scripture with you.
You can demonstrate that the Gospel you proclaim is also the Gospel shaping the way you live.
And you can trust God with what only God can do.
This is where the story turns from conviction toward hope.
Because perhaps you've already failed.
Perhaps you're remembering the calls you ignored.
The conversations you avoided.
The harsh words you spoke.
The years you spent pursuing recognition while neglecting people who loved you.
Perhaps someone is no longer here, and you cannot go back and give them the time you wish you had given.
That kind of regret can cut deeply.
And no inspirational sentence can simply erase it.
But listen to what the Gospel actually announces.
Jesus Christ did not come only for people who have always loved well.
He came to save sinners.
People who have been selfish.
People who have been proud.
People who have failed to show mercy.
People who have wounded others.
People who need forgiveness as desperately as the people they are called to love.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we earned the right to be loved.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And the Greek word behind “commendeth,” συνίστησιν (synistēsin), carries the sense of demonstrating or showing.
God demonstrated His love.
Not merely by announcing it.
But through the sacrificial death of His Son.
At the cross, the love of God was not an abstract idea.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that you can become good enough to deserve God's acceptance.
But that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior for those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
And when His grace takes hold of a life, it begins to change how that person lives.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly in every area.
But genuinely.
A proud person begins learning humility.
A bitter person begins learning forgiveness.
A selfish person begins learning generosity.
A distracted person begins learning to notice.
A person who once used others for recognition begins learning to serve without applause.
That is transformation.
Not a polished religious image.
A life being renewed by Christ.
And this is why our message remains:
He does not rewrite the past by pretending our sins never happened.
He does not call evil good.
He does not promise that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
But He forgives repentant sinners, makes them new in Himself, and teaches them to walk in righteousness.
And where reconciliation is possible, His grace can lead us toward confession, restitution, forgiveness, and the patient rebuilding of trust.
There is a beautiful Greek word in Ephesians 2:10.
ποίημα (poiēma).
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — KJV
The word poiēma means something made or created, a work of craftsmanship.
In Christ, believers are God's workmanship.
Notice the order.
We are not saved because our good works make us worthy.
Ephesians 2:8–9 explicitly teaches salvation by grace through faith, not as the result of works.
Then verse 10 tells us that those who are saved are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Good works follow as its fruit.
We don't love people to purchase God's approval.
We love because we have been loved by God.
We don't serve to become our own saviors.
We serve because Jesus is our Savior.
And we don't need to make every act of kindness into a grand spiritual production.
Sometimes the holiest response to a hurting person is simply to be present, tell the truth, and love them well.
Maybe tonight, the most important thing you do will not be posting another Christian message.
Maybe it will be putting your phone down and listening to your child.
Maybe it will be calling your father.
Maybe it will be asking your spouse, “Have I made you feel alone lately?”
Maybe it will be admitting, “I was wrong, and I'm sorry.”
Maybe it will be reaching out to someone you have neglected.
Maybe it will be visiting a lonely person.
Maybe it will be forgiving someone while still maintaining the boundaries wisdom requires.
Maybe it will be inviting a friend to hear the Gospel.
Or perhaps, after years of trying to look spiritually strong, it will be admitting that you are the one who needs help.
Because the Gospel does not merely send us to care for others.
It also teaches us to receive grace, to confess our need, and to depend upon the body of Christ.
You do not have to pretend you're fine.
You do not have to keep performing strength.
You can come to Jesus with empty hands.
And you can begin again.
If this article has exposed something you've been avoiding, don't rush past that conviction.
Bring it before the Lord.
Ask Him to show you where repentance is needed.
Ask Him to give you courage to repair what can be repaired.
Ask Him to make your love more than a collection of beautiful words.
And then consider one person.
Not twenty.
Not a whole audience.
One.
Whose burden could you help carry today?
Whose voice have you stopped hearing?
Who needs an apology rather than another explanation?
Who needs your presence more than your advice?
Who needs to hear about the hope found in Jesus Christ?
You may discover that your next opportunity to serve God is closer than you imagined.
Or, if you're carrying regret over someone you've neglected, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You don't need to reveal private details or expose someone else's pain.
You can be honest without making your wounds a public spectacle.
And if God has used an ordinary person to show you extraordinary kindness, consider sharing a short testimony. Someone reading the comments may need to be reminded that faithful love still exists.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to correct publicly.
Someone you genuinely love.
“I thought of you, and I thank God you're in my life.”
One thoughtful share may open a conversation you never expected.
And if you believe this kind of Scripture-centered message should continue reaching more people, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing words that make people emotional for a moment.
Our desire is to point people to Jesus Christ, encourage repentance and faith, strengthen believers through Scripture, and help people grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
It can be part of your Christian generosity and stewardship, alongside the responsibilities and giving commitments you already have.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, not under compulsion. Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That matters.
You cannot purchase God's favor through a monthly payment.
Think of it not as paying for God's blessing, but as voluntarily helping sustain and expand a ministry whose message you value.
These products are not the reason to follow Jesus.
You can still participate meaningfully.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and apply the Scriptures we share.
And above all, live the truth you are learning.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to point people toward the Savior who alone can forgive sin, restore the broken, and transform human lives.
The glory belongs to Jesus.
Always.
And now, before you close this article, return to the prayer that started everything.
“Lord, use me.”
Perhaps you prayed it this morning.
Perhaps you've prayed it for years.
Pray it again.
But this time, don't immediately imagine a stage.
Don't immediately imagine a crowd.
Don't immediately imagine a ministry known around the world.
Picture your home.
Your family.
Your neighbors.
Your coworkers.
Your church.
The people whose names are already written into the ordinary pages of your life.
And ask the Lord to give you eyes that truly see them.
Ask Him for a heart that responds with compassion.
Ask Him for the humility to repent where you have failed.
Ask Him for the courage to speak of Christ when the opportunity comes.
And ask Him for the faithfulness to love even when nobody is watching.
Because one day, the opportunities you keep postponing may no longer be available.
There are conversations that cannot be recovered.
Moments that cannot be repeated.
People we cannot hold onto forever.
So don't wait for a perfect season to begin obeying a clear command.
Don't wait until you have a platform to become a servant.
Don't wait until the world knows your name to love the person who already knows it.
You may never preach before thousands.
You may never write a bestselling book.
You may never become famous for your faith.
But you can still follow Jesus faithfully.
You can still speak the Gospel.
You can still love your neighbor.
You can still be present for someone who is suffering.
And you can still make a difference that eternity alone will fully reveal.
So tonight, when you pray, “Lord, use me,” leave room for a quieter answer.
Not necessarily a new destination.
Not necessarily a bigger assignment.
Perhaps simply a renewed heart for the people who are already there.
Because the person you keep overlooking may be praying for the very love you've been asking God to teach you how to give.
